findings.title: Rotating recovery codes into user storage leaves old local codes valid
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential treats a true result from user.credentialManager().updateCredential as done and returns without deleting recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local database. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential path is skipped in that branch, and nothing else removes those rows. Federated users who already had recovery codes locally (the only option before their user-storage provider accepted this type, or if another API wrote them locally) and then regenerate will keep the old set. UserCredentialManager.isValid accepts a code if any supporting CredentialInputValidator accepts it, and the local recovery-code provider validates local credentials independently of user storage, so the retired codes still authenticate after rotation. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential also prefers the federated credential, so the login form can show the new code number while the old codes still work. The same gap exists in the other direction: if updateCredential returns false but user storage already holds codes, the fallback local create adds a second valid set and does not disable the user-storage one. After a successful user-storage write the helper must remove existing local recovery-authn-codes credentials, and when falling back to local storage it must disable the user-storage credential, so only one set remains valid.

findings.title: Spent federated recovery codes are not removed and the next login crashes
findings.body: After a recovery code is accepted, the authenticator reloads the credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which now returns a user-storage credential ahead of a local one. If that model reports all codes used, it calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes credentials in Keycloak's local credential store; a federated credential id is not there, so the call is a no-op and the user-storage credential stays configured. isConfiguredFor therefore remains true. CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES is added, but required actions run only after the browser flow succeeds. On the next login the recovery-code authenticator still runs and constructs RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean, which unconditionally calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java line 21). With no unused code left that throws NoSuchElementException, the user gets an error page, and never reaches the setup action. If the browser flow requires recovery codes, they cannot sign in. Spent federated credentials have to be removed through the user-storage disable path (disableCredentialType or an equivalent federated remove), not only removeStoredCredentialById. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.disableCredentialType (line 217) currently ignores recovery-authn-codes, so that provider must clear them as well or this path cannot be fixed end to end.

findings.title: User-storage recovery codes are stored in cleartext and never consumed
findings.body: updateCredential writes input.getChallengeResponse() — the JSON array of raw recovery codes from CredentialHelper — straight into credentialData (line 197). isValid deserializes that list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted code. It does not delete the matched code, mark it used, or require the next unused code. getCredentials then rebuilds the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (line 237), which hashes the original list, marks every code unused, and does not copy the id that was stored on the saved credential. disableCredentialType (line 217) and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream (line 259) only handle OTP, so recovery codes cannot be disabled from account or admin APIs. Local recovery codes are hashed and one-time; this provider keeps plaintext codes valid for the life of the server-side user map, the login form always asks for code 0, and the authenticator's all-codes-used branch is unreachable. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only submits the first code once, so it passes even though the same code can be replayed.
